CONTEXT (include none of this as findings; it frames fit): We operate an LLM-agent-run product-development system ("shopsystem") that is re-founding its quality layer on the principle that construction definitions precede checks: every activity gets (a) an explicit definition of good construction compiled into the generating agent's context (role prompts define standing identity/cross-activity clarity; discrete skills capture individual activities), and (b) mechanical checks and review rubrics DERIVED from those definitions. We must choose FORMATS for a seed layer: process definitions (definition-level, NOT a workflow-engine prescription; must carry expected outcomes/outputs and resulting actions, including termination for long-running loops), role definitions, artifact/document-type schema definitions, principle statements, content-quality guidelines, and SMALL qualitative fitness-test sets for non-deterministic LLM-generated output. STRONG PREFERENCE: adopt established external standards/forms rather than inventing bespoke ones; bespoke requires justification. EVIDENCE BAR: primary sources and named methodologies/standards (not just popularized books); separate DESCRIBING a practice from RECOMMENDING its adoption; never cite a source you have not confirmed exists. You have web access: if WebSearch/WebFetch are not already available, load them via ToolSearch with query "select:WebSearch,WebFetch".

TASK: Survey established meta-models and standards for DEFINING processes, roles, and work products/artifacts — the formats themselves, not the methodologies' content. Cover at minimum (verify each; add others you find): ISO/IEC TR 24774 (guidelines for process description — title/purpose/outcomes/activities format), OMG SPEM 2.0 and Eclipse Process Framework method-content vs process separation, RUP's role/activity/artifact structure, ITIL process definition format (purpose/scope/inputs/outputs/triggers/roles), CMMI process-area structure (goals/practices), ISO/IEC 33001/15504 process assessment models, IEEE/ISO 12207 & 15288 process outcome conventions, BPMN/CMMN positioned at definition level only. For each: exactly what elements its definition format contains, citation, and fit for a lightweight LLM-agent-operated system wanting definition-level process specs WITHOUT prescribing a workflow engine.

Based on the search results, here's information about OMG SPEM 2.0 specification regarding method content, process separation, roles, tasks, and work products:

## Method Content vs. Process

The elements of SPEM can be categorized into method contents or processes. Method content are the roles defining development skills and responsibilities, tasks that those roles perform, and artifacts or work products that are the inputs and outputs of the tasks.

Processes reuse these method content elements and relate them into partially-ordered sequences that are customized to specific types of projects, providing clear separation of method content definitions from the development process application of method content.

## Key Structural Elements

The elements of a given method content are assets to be combined and included into any process. A development process is a sequence of tasks performed by roles and makes explicit how work products are created and evolve over time.

## Content Guidance

A SPEM 2.0 user can define Method Content as general guidance and build up a knowledge base of development methods without ever creating a process. Additionally, Roles or Work Products have descriptive text associated that textually define the element as well as providing guidance on how to use it.

## Key Improvement in SPEM 2.0

The latest SPEM version improves methodology content and process re-usability, by introducing new capabilities as a clear separation between structural and dynamic methodology concerns.

Based on the search results, here's information about OMG Essence kernel components:

## Overview

The Essence Kernel is from the SEMAT initiative by the Object Management Group, which aims to provide a theoretical basis to support comparison, evaluation and tailoring of software practices.

## Kernel Components

The kernel comprises Alphas (attributes relating to assessing project health), Activity spaces (the essential things to do) and Competencies (key capabilities required).

### Alphas

Alphas capture the main software engineering concepts along with predefined states and checklists, thus providing critical indicators for the measurement of project health. There are seven alphas: opportunity, stakeholders, requirements, software system, work, team, and way of working.

Each alpha is assigned a set of states that are used to determine the progress on each alpha during the SE endeavor, and each state includes a brief, general description and state checklists to help gauge whether the particular state has been reached.

### Activity Spaces

Activity Spaces describe the essential activities that need to be performed during software development and complement Alphas by focusing on the "doings" of a project, offering an activity-centric view.

### Competencies

Competencies represent the skills and abilities required to successfully perform software engineering tasks. The competencies underline the key capabilities required from the team in order to carry out the endeavor.

## Overview

ISO/IEC 15504 has been superseded by ISO/IEC 33001:2015 Information technology – Process assessment – Concepts and terminology as of March, 2015.

## Purpose and Concepts

ISO/IEC 33001:2015 is an international standard that provides key terminology and concepts related to process assessment in information technology, and outlines the framework for assessing process quality characteristics and the application of assessment results for process management. More specifically, it gives overall information on the concepts of process assessment, the application of process assessment for evaluating the achievement of process quality characteristics, and the application of the results of process assessment to the conduct of process management.

## Scope and Key Concepts

The ISO/IEC 330xx family enlarges the ISO/IEC 15504 application field and scope and focuses on the key concepts of process reference model, process assessment model and process measurement framework.

## Improvements Over ISO/IEC 15504

The new ISO/IEC 330xx family of standards presents a more detailed and well-defined process assessment model than the older ISO/IEC 15504 family, with the gaps regarding rating methods and aggregation methods perceived in the older standard now resolved with clear and standardized guidance, and definitions of some process attributes, outcomes and base practices now more consistent.

## ITIL Process Definition

An ITIL process is formally defined as "a structured set of Activities designed to accomplish a specific Objective. A Process takes one or more defined inputs and turns them into defined outputs."

## Core Components

**Purpose & Objectives:**
A process is organized around a set of objectives. The output produced by a process has to conform to operational norms that are derived from business objectives.

**Scope:**
A process may include any of the Roles, responsibilities, tools and management Controls required to reliably deliver the outputs.

**Inputs:**
Inputs are data or information used by the process and may be the output from another process. Inputs include information or requests that trigger the process (e.g., incident reports).

**Triggers:**
A process, or an activity within a process, is initiated by a trigger. A process may be ongoing or iterative, but it should be traceable to a specific trigger.

**Outputs:**
The main outputs from the process should be driven by the objectives and should include process measurements (metrics), reports and process improvement.

**Roles:**
Roles include assigned responsibilities such as service desk agents or managers.

**Metrics:**
Metrics are performance indicators like resolution time or customer satisfaction. Based on the output achieved, the process control measures the process to check if it is meeting its objectives and provides inputs that are needed for process improvements.

## Core Structure: "Who, How, What, When"

The Rational Unified Process describes who is doing what, how, and when using five primary elements: Roles (the who), Activities (the how), Artifacts (the what), Workflows (the when), and Disciplines (the "container" for the preceding four kinds of element).

**Roles**: An activity is a unit of work, composed of steps, that is performed by a role.

**Artifacts**: An artifact is an element of information that is the responsibility of a role and that is produced or consumed by activities. Artifacts are the tangible products of the project and are used as input by workers to perform an activity and are the result or output of such activities.

**Disciplines**: A discipline provides a view into the underlying process elements within RUP from the perspective of a general discipline of skills, describing a set of associated activities and artifacts based around a common skillset.

The Entry, Task, Verification, and Exit (ETVX) paradigm is a concept initially developed by a group at IBM, Radice et al.

The 'E' stands for the entry criteria which must be satisfied before a set of tasks can be performed, 'T' is the set of tasks to be performed, 'V' stands for the verification & validation process to ensure that the right tasks are performed, and 'X' stands for the exit criteria or the outputs of the tasks.

ETVX uses a simple technique of identifying the four important phases of any activity at a sub process level. These four phases of any activity are Entry Criteria, Tasks to be performed, Exit Criteria and Validation, Verification Conditions for each task.

The ETVX (Entry-Task-Validation-Exit) method describes processes through diagrams that show the entry conditions, tasks to be performed, validation of tasks, and exit conditions.

## Overview

ISO/IEC 24744:2014 introduces the Software Engineering Metamodel for Development Methodologies (SEMDM), a comprehensive metamodel that makes use of a new approach to defining methodologies based on the concept of powertype.

## Purpose and Application

The aim of SEMDM is to define methodologies in information-based domains, i.e. areas characterized by their intensive reliance on information management and processing, such as software, business or systems engineering.

## Key Problem It Solves

Development methodologies may be described in the context of an underpinning metamodel, but the precise mechanisms that permit them to be defined in terms of their metamodels are usually difficult to explain and do not cover all needs. For example, it is difficult to devise a practice that allows the definition of properties of the elements that compose the methodology and, at the same time, of the entities (such as work products) created when the methodology is applied.

## Harmonization Goal

Various methodologies are defined, used, or implied by a growing number of standards, and it is desirable that the concepts used by each methodology be harmonized. A vehicle for harmonization is the SEMDM. Conformance to this metamodel will ensure a consistent approach to defining each methodology with consistent concepts and terminology.

## Architecture

The SEMDM employs a three-level layered metamodel structure aligned with common metamodelling conventions. The M3 level serves as the metametamodel, defining the SEMDM itself through a set of foundational classes and relationships that describe how methodologies are modeled.

input.area_summary: The standards world already solved this exact problem — defining processes at definition level, without a workflow engine — and converged on one dominant convention plus two complementary meta-models. (1) The ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 line is the strongest adopt: ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774:2021 is a purpose-built specification for process description whose required elements are exactly name/purpose/outcomes with optional activities/tasks/inputs/outputs/controls; ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207 are the large worked corpus written in that format; and the ISO/IEC 330xx (ex-15504) assessment standards institutionalize precisely the shop's founding principle — checks (assessment indicators, process attributes) are formally DERIVED from the purpose+outcomes definitions, never freestanding. (2) OMG SPEM 2.0 (and its EPF Composer implementation, descended from RUP's role/activity/artifact triad) contributes the method-content-vs-process separation: reusable role/task/work-product/guidance definitions kept strictly apart from any ordering or lifecycle — a direct match for role prompts + discrete skills vs orchestration, adoptable as an organizing principle without the MOF metamodel. (3) OMG Essence 1.2 is the sleeper hit for the fitness-test requirement: alphas with named states, each state carrying a short qualitative checklist, and activities whose completion criteria are expressed in terms of those states — an established, standardized form for small qualitative fitness-test sets and loop-termination conditions. For artifact schemas, ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289's seven generic document types with per-item content requirements is the established form. ETVX (IBM, 1985) is the lightest credible per-activity frame (entry/task/verification/exit) when 24774 is too ceremonial. The notations — BPMN, CMMN, IDEF0 — and PMBOK's ITTOs are context-only: they describe flow or I/O, carry no purpose/outcome semantics, and (BPMN especially) pull toward engine execution. Recommended composite, each part standards-anchored: 24774-style purpose+outcomes for process definitions, with ETVX-style exit criteria for loop termination; SPEM's content/process split for roles-and-skills vs process specs; 15289-style generic-type+content schemas for artifacts; Essence-style state checklists (or Scrum-style Definition of Done commitments) for the qualitative fitness-test sets, from which review rubrics derive the way 330xx derives assessment indicators.

REQUIRED: process outcomes (short list of observable, assessable results — 'An X is produced/defined' declarative form)
OPTIONAL: process activities (cohesive groupings of tasks)

OPTIONAL: notes

It is definition-level by construction: purpose+outcomes carry 'expected outcomes/outputs' natively, and outcomes being observable/assessable is exactly the hook from which mechanical checks and review rubrics can be derived (the 330xx family does precisely this derivation). It deliberately says nothing about sequencing engines. Gap to cover by extension: no first-class 'resulting actions / termination condition' element for long-running loops — the controls-and-constraints and outcomes slots can host these, or borrow ETVX exit criteria. Method Content: Work Product Definition (artifact/deliverable/outcome kinds)
Method Content: Guidance — typed attachments including guideline, CHECKLIST, template, example, concept, report
Process side: Activity, Role Use, Task Use, Work Product Use — occurrences of content elements in an ordered structure
Process patterns for reusable process chunks
Managed textual descriptions attached to every element (purpose, brief description, main description)
findings.fit_notes: The method-content/process separation is a direct structural match for the shop: role prompts and discrete skills are Method Content; any process definition is a separate layer that references them — and SPEM proves you can maintain a full knowledge base of definitions 'without ever creating a process.' Checklist-as-first-class-guidance-type is also a precedent for attaching fitness-test sets to definitions. Adapt, don't adopt wholesale: the MOF/UML metamodel, compliance points, and XMI serialization are heavyweight tooling concerns; take the element taxonomy and the separation principle. Known weakness (which motivated Essence): SPEM has no semantic slot for outcomes/goals or progress/health — pair it with 24774-style outcomes.

findings.name: Eclipse Process Framework (EPF) Composer / Unified Method Architecture
findings.tradition: Eclipse open-source tooling implementing SPEM (IBM RUP lineage)
findings.citation: Eclipse Process Framework Project (EPF), Eclipse Foundation; EPF Composer authoring tool implementing the UMA/SPEM 2.0 metamodel; ships the OpenUP method library as its exemplar.
findings.what_it_defines: The working proof of SPEM's separation: method plugins hold reusable role/task/work-product/guidance content; Capability Patterns are reusable process chunks; Delivery Processes are full lifecycles assembled by binding patterns. Publishes method content as a static HTML site — definitions as browsable documents, no engine.
form_elements: Method library / method plugin packaging of content
Role, Task (with steps), Work Product, Guidance pages with standard description fields
Capability Pattern: reusable cluster of activities for one area of concern
Delivery Process: full lifecycle assembled from patterns via work-breakdown structure
Published static-site output of the whole method (content without execution)
findings.fit_notes: Context rather than adoption: the Eclipse tool itself is dormant Java tooling nobody should build on in 2026. Its value to the shop is as an existence proof and design reference — a mature system where definition documents (roles, tasks, artifacts, checklists) compile into an agent-consumable (here, human-consumable) corpus with processes strictly layered on top. The plugin/library packaging idea loosely parallels the shop's skills-plus-role-prompts compilation model.

findings.name: Rational Unified Process (RUP) — role/activity/artifact static structure
findings.tradition: Rational/IBM software process engineering (predecessor of SPEM and EPF)
findings.citation: Kruchten, P., The Rational Unified Process: An Introduction, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 2003 — ch. 3 'Static Structure: Process Description' defines the element model; also IBM Rational Method Composer product documentation.
findings.what_it_defines: The original commercial articulation of process-as-structured-content: 'who is doing what, how, and when' via Roles (who), Activities with steps (how), Artifacts (what), Workflows (when), grouped into Disciplines. Every artifact has a responsible role, a template, and review checkpoints; every role lists responsibilities and required skills.
form_elements: Role: responsibilities + required competencies/skills
Activity: unit of work performed by one role, decomposed into steps (thinking/performing/reviewing)
Artifact: information element with exactly one responsible role, produced/consumed by activities; carries templates and checkpoints (review checklists)
Workflow: sequencing view over activities (kept separate from the definitions)
Discipline: skillset-based container grouping roles/activities/artifacts
findings.fit_notes: Historically the template everything else formalized (SPEM/EPF/UMA are its descendants), so mostly context. Two forms remain directly reusable: (a) the one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule, a clean accountability convention for artifact schema definitions; (b) artifact 'checkpoints' — per-artifact review checklists shipped with the artifact definition — a direct precedent for deriving review rubrics from artifact schemas. RUP's content is proprietary IBM material and its lifecycle prescriptions are irrelevant here.

findings.name: OMG Essence 1.2 — Kernel and Language for Software Engineering Methods (SEMAT)
findings.citation: Object Management Group, Essence — Kernel and Language for Software Engineering Methods, Version 1.2, OMG document formal/18-10-02, 2018; Essence 2.0 in beta at OMG as of 2025.
findings.what_it_defines: A standard for defining practices and methods around progress and health rather than workflow: Alphas (essential things whose state you track) each have an ordered set of named states, and each state carries a short qualitative CHECKLIST; Activity Spaces name essential things to do; Competencies name required capabilities with levels; a composition language assembles practices into methods.
form_elements: Alpha: essential trackable concern (kernel's seven: Opportunity, Stakeholders, Requirements, Software System, Team, Work, Way of Working)
Alpha state: named progress/health state with a checklist of a few plainly-worded criteria per state
Work product: described artifact with levels of detail, attached to alphas as evidence
Activity: has completion criteria expressed in terms of alpha states and work-product levels of detail — i.e., termination conditions defined by state, not by step count
Activity space: placeholder for essential work, method-agnostic
Competency: capability with five achievement levels
Practice/Method: composable units — a method is a composition of practices over the kernel
Card-based presentation format (state cards with checklists) designed for at-a-glance use
findings.fit_notes: The strongest external answer to two of the seed layer's hardest requirements. (a) Small qualitative fitness-test sets for non-deterministic output: alpha-state checklists are exactly that form, standardized — short, ordinal, qualitative, judged not computed. (b) Termination for long-running loops: Essence activities complete when target alpha states are reached, which is a definition-level termination semantic needing no engine. Adapt rather than adopt: keep the state+checklist+completion-criteria FORM, replace the software-endeavor kernel alphas with shop-native ones (e.g., Intent, Scenario Set, Dispatch, Reconciliation). Recent literature already explores LLM agents consuming Essence practice descriptions.

findings.name: CMMI model structure — goals/practices (V1.3) and practice areas with intent/value (V3.0)
findings.tradition: SEI/Carnegie Mellon capability maturity tradition, now ISACA
findings.citation: CMMI for Development, Version 1.3, CMU/SEI-2010-TR-033, Software Engineering Institute, 2010 (process area = purpose statement, specific goals/practices, generic goals/practices, informative subpractices and example work products); CMMI Model V3.0, ISACA, 2023 (practice areas with intent/value statements and practice-group levels).
findings.what_it_defines: A model format built on a required/expected/informative trichotomy: goals (required — what must be true) are distinct from practices (expected — typical ways to achieve them), which are distinct from informative material (subpractices, example work products). V3.0 recast this as practice areas carrying an intent statement + value statement + required info, with practices in evolutionary practice-group levels.
form_elements: Process area / practice area: named cluster with purpose or intent statement
V3.0: value statement per practice area and per practice (why it matters, outcome-linked)
Specific goals (required component) vs specific practices (expected component) — achievement of the goal, not performance of the practice, is what is assessed
Generic goals/practices: institutionalization criteria applied uniformly across areas
Informative components: subpractices, notes, example work products, elaborations
V3.0 practice group levels 1–5: evolutionary layering where each level subsumes the lower
findings.fit_notes: Two adaptable forms: (a) the required/expected/informative trichotomy is a precise instrument for the shop's definitions — separating what must be true of a construction (checkable) from typical ways to construct it (guidance) prevents rubrics from ossifying implementation detail; (b) V3.0's intent+value statement pair is a compact established header for any definition. Reject the surrounding machinery (maturity levels, appraisal method, organizational institutionalization) as scale-inappropriate; CMMI is an appraisal model, not a process-definition format, so it earns adapt only for these structural devices.

findings.name: ITIL process description format (v3) and ITIL 4 practice guides
findings.tradition: UK OGC / AXELOS / PeopleCert IT service management
findings.citation: ITIL Service Design, 2011 edition, Cabinet Office/TSO (per-process description convention: purpose/objectives, scope, value, policies, activities, triggers/inputs/outputs/interfaces, CSFs/KPIs, roles); ITIL Foundation: ITIL 4 Edition, AXELOS, 2019, and the PeopleCert ITIL 4 practice guides (34 management practices).
findings.what_it_defines: v3: a fixed per-process documentation template — every process described with the same section skeleton including measurable success criteria. ITIL 4: replaced 'processes' with 'practices' (capability bundles), each documented in a standard practice-guide structure spanning the four dimensions of service management.
form_elements: v3 per process: purpose and objectives; scope; value to business; policies/principles/basic concepts; process activities, methods, techniques; triggers, inputs, outputs, interfaces to other processes; information management; critical success factors (CSFs) with key performance indicators (KPIs) nested under each; challenges and risks
Roles bound via responsibility (RACI) matrices rather than embedded in the process text

ITIL 4 per practice guide: general information (purpose, key terms, practice success factors with key metrics); value streams and processes (activities with inputs/outputs, value-stream contribution); organizations and people (roles, competency profiles); information and technology; partners and suppliers
findings.fit_notes: Describing more than recommending: ITIL's template discipline — every process/practice documented in the identical section skeleton, with success factors and metrics nested under the definition — is a good pattern precedent, and its trigger element covers the seed layer's 'resulting actions' need better than the ISO line does. Its practice-success-factor → key-metric nesting is another instance of checks-derived-from-definitions. Reasons to only adapt: content is IT-operations-specific, the corpus is commercial/licensed (not freely citable text), and ITIL 4's practice guides are long-form prose, heavier than a lightweight seed layer wants.

findings.name: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289 — Content of life-cycle information items (documentation)
findings.tradition: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 + IEEE systems & software engineering
findings.citation: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289:2019, Systems and software engineering — Content of life-cycle information items (documentation), 4th ed. (earlier editions 2011, 2015, 2017).
findings.what_it_defines: The standard meta-format for artifact/document-type schemas: every information item is classified as one of seven generic document types, and then given specific required-content clauses. Explicitly medium-independent — an information item may live in a repository, be split, or be combined; the schema defines content, not packaging.
form_elements: Seven generic types: description, plan, policy, procedure, report, request, specification
Generic content requirements per type (e.g., every plan carries scope, approach, schedule, resources, risks)
Specific content requirements per named information item (e.g., what a test plan or an architecture description must contain)
Mapping tables from information items to the 12207/15288 processes that produce/consume them
Rule that items are defined 'as if a separate document' but may be aggregated or stored as records
findings.fit_notes: Direct adopt for the artifact/document-type schema slot in the seed layer: the two-level scheme (generic type → specific required content) is exactly a document schema definition, and the process↔information-item mapping tables are the established way to state 'this process yields these artifacts' — tying process outcomes to artifact schemas so checks can validate both together. The shop's existing kind-schema/template mechanism (write-* skills) is already isomorphic to this; 15289 supplies the external standard to anchor it. Its specific item catalog (test plans, QA records) is domain content to ignore.

findings.name: ETVX — Entry / Task / Verification / eXit process-definition paradigm
findings.tradition: IBM programming process architecture (CMM-era process definition)
findings.citation: Radice, R.A., Roth, N.K., O'Hara, A.C., Ciarfella, W.A., 'A Programming Process Architecture', IBM Systems Journal, vol. 24, no. 2, 1985 — origin of the ETVX paradigm, widely reused in SEI/CMM-lineage process definition guidance.
findings.what_it_defines: The minimal per-activity definition cell: Entry criteria that must hold before work starts; the Task set; Verification steps confirming the right tasks were done right; eXit criteria that must hold for the activity to be complete. Composable into larger processes by chaining cells; no ordering engine implied.
form_elements: Entry criteria (preconditions on inputs/state, including triggers)
Task list (what is performed)
Verification/validation conditions (checks bound to the tasks)
Exit criteria (postconditions/outputs that define 'done')
findings.fit_notes: The lightest credible established form in the survey, and the only classic one that builds verification INTO the definition cell — matching 'definitions precede checks' at the single-activity grain. Exit criteria are a ready-made termination construct for long-running loops (loop until exit criteria hold), and entry criteria give 'resulting actions' their trigger side. Adopt as the per-activity inner structure inside 24774-style process definitions (24774 gives the process header — purpose/outcomes; ETVX gives each activity its entry/verify/exit contract). Caveat: primary 1985 paper is paywalled IBM Systems Journal material; the paradigm itself is thoroughly documented in secondary process-engineering literature.

findings.name: BPMN 2.0 — Business Process Model and Notation (definition-level positioning)
findings.citation: OMG, Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Version 2.0, formal/2011-01-03; published as ISO/IEC 19510:2013. Conformance clause distinguishes Process Modeling Conformance (descriptive/analytic sub-classes) from Process Execution Conformance.
findings.what_it_defines: A graphical notation plus XML interchange format for control-flow process models: activities, events, gateways, sequence/message flows, pools/lanes, data objects. The spec itself stratifies usage — a Descriptive conformance sub-class exists precisely for documentation-level modeling with no execution semantics exercised.
form_elements: Flow objects: activities/tasks, events (start/intermediate/end, incl. timer/message/error), gateways (exclusive/parallel/inclusive/event-based)
Swimlanes: pools and lanes assigning flow to participants/roles
Data objects, data stores, messages
Sequence flow and message flow connectors
Descriptive vs Analytic vs Common Executable conformance sub-classes
XML process-definition interchange format
findings.fit_notes: Context-only, on the task's own framing. BPMN answers 'in what order does control flow' — it has no slots for purpose, outcomes, quality criteria, or role/artifact definitions, so it cannot carry a construction definition; and its center of gravity (execution semantics, engine interchange) is exactly the workflow-engine prescription the shop is avoiding. Legitimate residual use: an occasional descriptive-class diagram inside a process definition when a handoff topology genuinely needs a picture — mermaid can render the equivalent without importing the standard.

findings.name: CMMN — Case Management Model and Notation
findings.tradition: OMG business modeling (declarative counterpart to BPMN)
findings.citation: OMG, Case Management Model and Notation (CMMN), Version 1.0, 2014 (current version 1.1 at omg.org/spec/CMMN); introductory treatment in Marin, 'Introduction to the Case Management Model and Notation (CMMN)', arXiv:1608.05011, 2016.
findings.what_it_defines: A declarative model for knowledge work where activity order is unpredictable: a case plan contains stages and tasks whose availability is governed by sentries (entry criteria) and exit criteria, plus milestones marking achieved states and discretionary items a knowledge worker may add at run time. Describes what is allowed/required, never a flow sequence.
form_elements: Case plan model containing stages (nestable) and tasks (human, process, case, decision)
Sentries: entry criteria and exit criteria on any plan item, combining events and conditions
Milestones: named achievable states with entry criteria (no work of their own)
Event listeners (timer, user)
Discretionary items and planning tables (run-time plan extension)
Case file items: the information the case works over
findings.fit_notes: Context-only as a notation to adopt (thin industry uptake, engine-flavored spec), but it is the standards world's clearest vocabulary for exactly the shop's situation: long-running, non-deterministic work defined by entry/exit criteria and milestones rather than sequences. Worth mining terminologically — 'milestone with entry criteria' and 'exit criterion on a stage' are precise, citable concepts for expressing loop termination and resulting actions in process definitions without any flow prescription. If a definition-level format for unpredictable work is ever needed wholesale, CMMN is the precedent to cite.

findings.name: IDEF0 — Integration Definition for Function Modeling (ICOM)
findings.tradition: US Air Force SADT lineage / NIST federal standard
findings.citation: NIST, Integration Definition for Function Modeling (IDEF0), FIPS PUB 183, 1993; also IEEE Std 1320.1-1998 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 31320-1:2012.
findings.what_it_defines: A function-decomposition format: each function is a box with typed arrows — Inputs (left, transformed), Controls (top, constrain/govern), Outputs (right, results), Mechanisms (bottom, who/what performs) — decomposed hierarchically (A0, A1, A11…) with strict syntax rules. Models what functions exist and what they consume/produce/obey, not when they run.
form_elements: Function box with verb-phrase name
ICOM arrows: Input, Control, Output, Mechanism (and Call)
Hierarchical decomposition with parent-child diagram numbering and arrow continuity rules
Node tree and glossary as required companion artifacts
Rule set limiting boxes per diagram (3–6) to force appropriate altitude
findings.fit_notes: Context-only. Genuinely definition-level and engine-free, and the Control-vs-Input distinction (a definition or policy that GOVERNS an activity vs material it transforms) is a conceptually sharp device — the shop's construction definitions are, in IDEF0 terms, Controls compiled into the generating agent's context. But it is a diagram grammar without purpose/outcome/quality elements, its practitioner base has aged out, and adopting it would add notation burden with no checking leverage. Useful as vocabulary, not as a format.

findings.name: PMBOK Guide ITTO process format (PMI)
findings.citation: Project Management Institute, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), Sixth Edition, 2017 — 49 processes each defined by Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs; superseded in emphasis by PMBOK Seventh Edition, 2021 (principles and performance domains, ITTOs dropped from the core).
findings.what_it_defines: Each process = a purpose paragraph plus three lists: Inputs (documents/plans consumed), Tools & Techniques (methods applied), Outputs (deliverables produced), with outputs of one process feeding inputs of others across five process groups and ten knowledge areas.
form_elements: Process purpose paragraph
Inputs list
Tools & techniques list
Outputs list
Cross-process input/output tracing (data-flow diagrams per process)
findings.fit_notes: Context-only. The ITTO frame is widely known and trivially lightweight, but it defines a process by its I/O signature alone — no outcomes, no completion or quality criteria, nothing derivable into checks — and PMI itself walked away from it in the Seventh Edition, which is a caution against adopting it now. Its one durable idea, explicit output-to-input tracing between processes, is already covered better by 15289's process↔information-item mapping.

findings.name: ISO/IEC 24744 — Metamodel for Development Methodologies (SEMDM)
findings.tradition: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 method engineering (academic method-engineering community)
findings.citation: ISO/IEC 24744:2014, Software engineering — Metamodel for development methodologies (first edition 2007), defining SEMDM via the powertype pattern.
findings.what_it_defines: A rival metamodel to SPEM that models the method domain AND the endeavor domain together: powertype pairs (e.g., WorkProductKind/WorkProduct) let one define both the kind (the schema, at method level) and the instances produced when the method is enacted, covering work units, work products, producers (roles/tools), and stages in one framework.
form_elements: Powertype pattern: paired Kind class (method level) and instance class (endeavor level) for every concept
Work units (tasks, techniques, processes)
Work products with kinds and status
Producers: roles, teams, tools
Stages: temporal method elements (phases, milestones) kept distinct from work units
findings.fit_notes: Context-only. Intellectually it addresses a problem the shop actually has — the same definition must both instruct generation (method level) and validate the generated instance (endeavor level), which is the powertype's exact job — so it is worth knowing the argument. But adoption fails the lightweight test decisively: SEMDM's uptake is essentially academic, tooling is nil, and its rigor overhead dwarfs the seed layer's needs. Cite it, if at all, as justification that definition-level and instance-level views of one concept belong in one artifact.

findings.name: Scrum Guide accountabilities and artifact commitments (Definition of Done)
findings.citation: Schwaber, K. and Sutherland, J., The Scrum Guide, November 2020, scrumguides.org — accountabilities replacing 'roles'; each artifact bound to a commitment (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done), with the Definition of Done as 'a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required'.
findings.what_it_defines: Two compact definitional forms inside a deliberately minimal framework document: (a) role definitions as short accountability lists — each accountability a bullet of what the holder is answerable for, not a task script; (b) every artifact paired with exactly one commitment — a small, binding qualitative criteria set that says when the artifact is acceptable, with DoD as the canonical example.
form_elements: Accountability list per role (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers): 4–8 bullets of answerable-for statements
Artifact + commitment pairing: Product Backlog→Product Goal, Sprint Backlog→Sprint Goal, Increment→Definition of Done
Definition of Done: enumerated qualitative quality measures; work not meeting it cannot be released and returns to the backlog (a built-in resulting-action rule)
Framework-level rule that the whole definition fits in ~13 pages (a lightness benchmark)
findings.fit_notes: Adapt. The artifact-plus-commitment pairing is the most widely operated real-world instance of the shop's exact pattern: a small qualitative fitness-test set attached to an artifact type, consulted by the producer during construction and by reviewers after — with a defined consequence when it fails (return to backlog = the resulting-action clause the seed layer wants). The accountability-list form is likewise a proven lightweight shape for role definitions feeding role prompts. These are practice forms, not schemas — pair them with 15289-style content schemas rather than replacing them.
